events.text: You have come a hand's width a year down the lane, and now you lie under the place where five roads meet: the road from the hills, the road to the river, the market road, the road to the county town, and the old road that goes past the graves. All day, feet. Straw sandals, ox hooves, cart wheels, a horse now and then. Every one of them is going somewhere else.

choices.text: Listen to where each road is going

effects.log: The hill road carries charcoal and firewood. The river road carries fish and gossip. The market road carries everything twice. The county road carries tax rice and bad news. The grave road carries the dead and those who miss them. You learn the five voices, and you never mistake them again.

choices.text: Warm the place where they cross

effects.log: Travellers start to stop at the crossroads without knowing why: to shift a pack, to retie a sandal, to sit a moment. The ground is warm there in every season. By the end of the year there is a bench, and then an old woman selling barley tea beside it.

choices.text: Settle deep and hold the crossing firm

effects.log: The ruts fill and do not come back. In the rainy season the five roads go to mud everywhere except in the middle, where they meet. Carters learn to make for the middle and wait there for the mud to dry. You hold them up, all of them, and it is not heavy yet.

events.text: A funeral bier comes down the grave road with its bell and its paper banners, and a wedding procession comes up the market road with its red sedan and its drummers, and they meet in the middle, right over you. Neither will give way. The mourners say the dead do not wait. The wedding party says the living have waited long enough.

choices.text: Let the dead go first

effects.log: You tilt the ground a hair toward the grave road, and the bier-bearers find themselves walking before they decide to. The wedding party grumbles and then bows its heads as the bier goes by. The bride, inside the sedan, is the only one who thinks it a good omen.

choices.text: Let the living go first

effects.log: The sedan-bearers find the road under them firm and easy and are across before anyone can argue. The mourners shout. Then the old man on the bier is carried past a wedding drum still beating, and his widow laughs out loud for the first time in a week.

choices.text: Shiver the ground so both stop, and bow to each other

effects.log: A small tremor, exactly in the middle. Both parties stop dead. In the silence somebody bows, and then everybody does: the mourners to the bride, the drummers to the bier. Then they go round each other, slowly, like water round a stone. The village tells it for a hundred years.

events.text: The village has set a guard at the crossroads against the bandits of the hill road: {npc}, a young villager with a spear and a lantern who sleeps on duty every single night, curled on the warm ground right over you, snoring at the stars.

choices.text: Keep {him} warm and keep watch yourself

mem.note: never once robbed on my watch

effects.log: Nobody is ever robbed at the crossroads on the nights {npc} sleeps there, which is all of them. {npc} gets a reputation as the best guard in the county and is honestly baffled by it.

choices.text: Wake {him} with a jolt whenever a stranger comes

effects.log: The ground jumps under the sleeper every time a footstep comes down the hill road. {npc} learns to wake at a touch, and then to sleep lightly, and in the end becomes a real guard, grumbling the whole way.

choices.text: Send {him} a dream of the road

effects.log: In the dream the five roads go on for ever, and at the end of each there is a different life. {npc} wakes at dawn and sits looking down each road in turn. That autumn {npc} leaves by the river road and does not come back for years.

events.text: A small child stands at the crossroads in the dusk, crying without any noise, the way lost children do when they have been crying a long time. Five roads, and the child came down one of them and does not know which.

choices.text: Warm the road home, only that one

effects.log: One road goes warm under the small bare feet. The child stops crying, considers, and walks up it, faster and faster. An hour later you feel a whole house running down the same road with torches, and meeting the child halfway.

choices.text: Keep the child warm in the middle until someone comes

effects.log: The child sits down on the warm spot and falls asleep. At midnight a frantic grandfather comes down the hill road with a torch and finds the child asleep in the exact middle of the crossroads, unharmed and quite warm. He never lets go of the small hand again, all the way home.

choices.text: Make the old tea-seller look up

effects.log: The tea-seller, packing up, feels the bench shiver and turns round and sees the child. Tea-sellers know every face on five roads. Within the hour the child is home, and the tea-seller has a story to tell for the rest of the season.

events.text: Travellers add a stone to the heap at the crossroads as they pass, for luck on the road: a pebble from the hill road, a smooth one from the river, a chip of roof-tile. The heap is waist-high now, with a straw rope round it and strips of cloth tied to a pole. The village has started calling the crossroads by a name, and the name is yours.

choices.text: Accept the stones, one by one

effects.log: Every stone is a small weight and a small wish, set down on you by somebody going somewhere else. You take each one. By the end of the year you know four hundred travellers by the stone they left, and you wish every one of them a dry road.

choices.text: Give a little luck back down each road

effects.log: No robbers on the hill road that year. No drowning at the river ford. No lame ox on the market road. The cairn grows faster. Luck, it turns out, is something people will happily carry stones for.

choices.text: Wonder whether a cairn is a gift or a load

effects.log: Both. You decide it is both. That is the first thing you learn about being honoured: it weighs something. You are not heavy yet. You can feel where the heaviness will come from.

events.text: Wood first. The spring in the valley does not end. The willows leaf, and leaf again; the barley shoots up too fast and falls over in the wind; the bamboo comes up through the floor of a farmer's storehouse. Everything green is pushing, and it is pushing against you.

choices.text: Hold the spring back, gently

effects.log: You set your weight against the pushing, the way a hand rests on a lid. The barley stops falling over. The bamboo stops at the storehouse floor and goes sideways, sulking. The year turns to summer a little late and a little steadier. (Wood -2, Earth +1)

choices.text: Let it feed the summer instead

effects.log: Wood feeds fire. You turn the push of the spring toward the summer, and the summer comes early and hot and the barley ripens all at once. The farmers are out in the fields by moonlight. (Wood -2, Fire +2)

choices.text: Let it grow. A strong spring is a good thing

effects.log: The valley is greener than anyone remembers. The orchards are a sea. Somewhere at the edge of your feeling a terrace wall bulges where the roots are getting into it. (Wood +2)

events.text: Fire. The smithy on the market road has a new bellows and a new smith who loves it. The forge is never cold. Sparks go up into the thatch of the next house every week, and the well water by the smithy is warm to the touch.

choices.text: Cool the ground under the forge

effects.log: The smith finds the forge sulky all season, slow to catch and quick to die down. The neighbours stop finding scorch marks in the thatch. Fire makes earth: some of the heat goes into you, and you are warmer for it. (Fire -2, Earth +1)

choices.text: Let the fire feed the earth

effects.log: You drink the forge-heat down through the floor of the smithy like a root drinking rain. The smith never knows why the forge is so steady. You grow. Earth grows. (Fire -1, Earth +2)

choices.text: Let it burn bright; the village needs ploughshares

effects.log: Every farmer in the valley has a new ploughshare by spring, and the smith is a rich man. A thatch catches once, and the whole street puts it out with buckets. (Fire +2, Metal +1)

events.text: Earth: your own. A great harvest, and then another. The granaries are full, the storehouses are full, the jars behind every house are full, and still the rice comes in. It is the earth phase swelling, and it is you, and it feels very good. In the next valley, a well has gone low.

choices.text: Give some of the plenty to metal: let them sell it

effects.log: Earth bears metal. The surplus goes to market and comes back as coin and iron and new tools. The granaries are merely full, not bursting. The next valley's well creeps back up a hand's width. (Earth -2, Metal +2)

choices.text: Keep it. A full granary is a full granary

effects.log: You lie heavy and content under a valley of full jars. It is the best year you have ever felt. In the next valley the well goes lower. Earth dams water. You know it, and you do not quite look at it. (Earth +2)

choices.text: Send the extra down into the deep wells

effects.log: You loosen your hold on the deep ground, and the water that you have been holding back without knowing it runs on into the wells of the next valley. Your own harvest is ordinary next year. Theirs is not a disaster. (Earth -2, Water +2)

events.text: Metal. Two families at the crossroads are feuding over a sword: an old blade dug out of a field that lies on the boundary of both. Knives come out at the well. The sword lies on a shrine shelf in neither house, waiting, and everything metal in the village feels sharper this year.

choices.text: Rust the sword overnight, so there is nothing to fight over

effects.log: In the morning the famous blade is a red flake of rust in the shape of a sword. Both families look at it for a long time. Then one of the grandfathers starts to laugh, and after a while the other does too. (Metal -2, Earth +1)

choices.text: Let the metal cool into water

effects.log: Metal gathers water. That autumn the dew lies heavy on every blade in the village, every hoe and every knife, and somehow nobody feels like drawing anything. The feud cools into a long sour silence, which is better. (Metal -2, Water +2)

choices.text: Let them fight it out

effects.log: They do, at the crossroads, over you. Nobody dies. Two men are carried home and a house burns. The sword goes to the magistrate, who keeps it. Everything metal is sharper still. (Metal +2)

events.text: Water. A wet summer, and then the river. It comes over the low fields in a night and stands brown in the paddies and in the market street and up to the knees of the stone cairn at the crossroads. It is pressing down on you from above, cold, heavy, everywhere.

choices.text: Rise and dam it: earth overcomes water

effects.log: You push up under the low fields like a back under a load, and the water runs off you toward the river, all of it, in a single morning. The village calls it a miracle. You feel it in your middle as a hard, dry ache. Earth overcomes water, and it is not gentle. (Water -3, Earth +1)

choices.text: Drink it slowly, and let it feed the wood

effects.log: Water feeds wood. You take the flood down into yourself and pass it on to every root in the valley. The fields drain in a week instead of a month, and next spring the orchards are astonishing. (Water -2, Wood +2)

choices.text: Let it stand. Floods leave good silt

effects.log: The water goes in its own time. It leaves a hand of black silt on every field, and the next harvest is a fat one. Five spokes, one hub. You begin to see: not one of them is the enemy. Only too much of any. (Water +1)

events.text: At the village gate, a little way up the road from you, stand the two carved posts: Great General Under Heaven, tall and fierce in a scholar's hat, and the General Under the Earth, shorter, rounder, with a painted grin. They have stood there longer than the oldest grandmother. The second one has noticed you, and has views about whose ground this is.

choices.text: Bow to them both, as the newcomer

effects.log: The tall one ignores you, as a general should. The short one looks surprised, and then very pleased with itself. Under the Earth is its title, after all. You let it think so. A post that keeps demons out of the village can think anything it likes.

choices.text: Explain, politely, that the ground goes down further than its feet

effects.log: The General Under the Earth is a post. Its feet go down a forearm into the clay, and below that it has never thought about. It thinks about it now. For a whole season its painted grin looks slightly less certain.

choices.text: Ignore them: they are only wood

effects.log: Only wood. That winter a fever comes up the road from the river and stops dead at the gate, and turns, and goes away up the hill road instead. You felt it stop. Only wood, you think, rather less certainly.

events.text: The village carves new posts at the first full moon, as it does every few years: two alder trunks, the faces cut with an adze, the eyes painted, the names written down the front in black ink. The old posts are laid in the ditch to rot. The new ones are sunk into the ground beside them, a forearm deep, into the clay that is the edge of you.

choices.text: Take the new posts in firmly

effects.log: They go in straight and stay straight. The carvers say these are the best-set posts in the county. The old General Under the Earth, in the ditch, rotting, says nothing at all. You keep a little warmth under it until it is gone.

choices.text: Hold the old posts up a little longer

effects.log: You warm the ditch so the old wood rots slowly, and for years four generals stand at the gate, two fierce and new and two grey and leaning. Travellers think the village is doubly protected. It is.

events.text: Something comes up the river road one night that is not a person: a cold, a sickness with a shape, walking. It reaches the gate and the posts. The General Under Heaven glares. The General Under the Earth grins its painted grin. The thing waits, testing. Their feet are in your ground.

choices.text: Lend the posts your strength through their feet

effects.log: You push up into the wood, and the two posts are suddenly very much more than wood. The thing at the gate steps back. It turns, and goes back down the river road, and the village has a winter without a single cough. The General Under the Earth is unbearable about it for years.

choices.text: Let the posts do their own work

ok.log: They do it. The thing waits all night and goes before dawn. You realise you did not need to do anything, and that this is a new feeling: something in your ground that holds up without you. You like it more than you expected.

fail.log: It gets past the short one. You catch it in the road beyond, in the clay, and hold it there until dawn burns it off. It costs you. Three houses cough for a month and nobody dies. (-6 health)

events.text: A travelling official has had the posts' faces painted over in plain white, because a fierce face at a gate is superstition, and superstition is bad for the county. The villagers are frightened. The General Under the Earth, faceless, has gone very quiet in your ground.

choices.text: Let the paint peel by spring

effects.log: The white flakes off in the first rain and the faces come through underneath, fiercer than before, as if they had been sharpening themselves under the paint. The villagers repaint them anyway, very bright. The official never comes back to check.

choices.text: Speak to the faceless one through the ground

effects.log: A face is only paint, you tell it. Its feet are still in the ground, and so is its work. The post is quiet for a long time. Then, very faintly, you feel it grin under the white. It does not need you to agree.

events.text: A young geomancer comes to the crossroads with an old compass, the many-ringed wooden kind, its needle wobbling. {npc} is the apprentice of an old geomancer who once walked this valley and said it had a navel. The old one is dead. The apprentice has the compass and the notes and a great deal to prove.

choices.text: Make the needle point straight down

mem.note: turned my compass down into the ground

effects.log: The needle swings, shivers, and points at the ground between {npc}'s knees, which no compass needle can do. {npc} sits back on both heels and stares at it. Then {npc} starts writing very fast.

choices.text: Let the compass find you honestly, in its own time

effects.log: It takes {npc} nine days of pacing and measuring and arguing with the old notes. On the ninth evening the lines on the map all meet at the crossroads, and {npc} laughs out loud and the tea-seller asks what is so funny.

choices.text: Send {him} up the lane to the farmhouse first

effects.log: {npc} goes back up the lane to the farmhouse in the old notes and finds a jar behind it with a straw cap, still warm. The family there tells stories. By the time {npc} comes back to the crossroads, there is a line on the map that runs from the jar to you.

events.text: {npc} has drawn the valley as a body: the hills for shoulders, the river for a vein, the crossroads for its navel. The map goes to the county town and is copied. People begin to come and stand at the crossroads to feel the luck of the centre. Some of them want to buy the land.

choices.text: Make the land too stony to build on

effects.log: Every buyer who digs a test pit hits stone a spade down, the hard kind, everywhere. The crossroads stays a crossroads. {npc} is accused of drawing a false map and does not mind at all.

choices.text: Let them come and stand, and be lucky

effects.log: They stand, and go home, and have their good years. The crossroads is famous for a while. A shrine goes up, small and crooked, built by the tea-seller's grandson. {npc} writes it all down.

choices.text: Shake the map in {npc}'s hands as a warning

effects.log: The paper jumps, and the ink of the navel runs in a little gold smear. {npc} looks at it a long time and then, quietly, makes no more copies. The ones already out are enough to make trouble, but less.

events.text: {npc} is old now, and has come back to the crossroads to die near the navel of the valley, which every geomancer secretly wants. A little shrine of stones and a straw rope, a bowl of water, and an old person sitting by it in the sun, talking to the ground as if it were a colleague.

choices.text: Answer, once, in warmth

effects.npcPass: old age, in the sun at the crossroads
effects.log: The stones of the little shrine go warm under {npc}'s hand. {npc} nods, as at a colleague who has finally agreed about something, and closes both eyes in the sun, and does not open them. The shrine stays. People call it the Navel.

choices.text: Keep the bowl of water clear for a season

effects.npcPass: old age, at the navel of the valley
effects.log: The water in the bowl never once has a leaf or a fly in it all summer. {npc} notices on the first day and smiles on every day after. In the autumn {npc} is gone, and the bowl is still clear.

events.text: Someone from the farmhouse up the lane comes down to the crossroads with a carrying frame: {npc}, of the family above the jar, going to the market alone. {npc} stops in the middle of the crossroads, for no reason {he} could name, and stands there feeling the ground, as the grandmother of that house once felt a jar.

choices.text: Warm the ground for {him}, like the jar

mem.note: warmed the crossroads like the jar at home

effects.log: {npc} puts a palm down flat on the road, in front of everyone, and takes it away and puts it back. Then {npc} grins, the grin of somebody who has found out a family secret, and goes to market whistling.

choices.text: Send {him} on to market with luck

effects.log: The best price in the market for {npc}'s beans, and a good word from a peddler, and a dry road home. {npc} tells the family it was a lucky day. The family looks at each other and does not say anything.

events.text: The family above the jar has started leaving a handful of the tenth-month rice at the crossroads cairn, as well as in the jar behind the house. Nobody told them to. {npc} does it on the way to market, every year, and bows once.

choices.text: Take the rice and keep both places warm

effects.log: The jar behind the house and the cairn at the crossroads: two homes, one handful each. You are stretched a little thinner and warmer than before. The family's luck does not change. It does not need to.

choices.text: Leave the rice for the birds, and the luck for the family

effects.log: Sparrows have the rice by noon. {npc} sees them at it and laughs, and does not mind. The old lord of the site has always been a little odd. The family's ox lives to thirty.

events.text: Word comes down the lane in the winter: the farmhouse is to be pulled down for a bigger one, and the jar behind it with it. The family argues for a week. The youngest says the jar stays. The eldest says a jar is a jar.

choices.text: Make the jar too warm to touch the day they come to move it

effects.log: Nobody will lift it. The new house is built round it, with a gap in the wall so the jar stays in the corner of the yard where it always was. The builder thinks the family is mad. The family thinks the builder is lucky not to have been bitten.

choices.text: Let them move it, and follow it

effects.log: They carry it ten paces to the new corner of the new yard, and you send a root after it through the clay, slowly, all winter. By spring it is warm again in its new place. A centre can move ten paces. You did not know that.

choices.text: Let the old jar go: you are under a crossroads now

effects.log: The old jar is broken in the rebuilding and the family buys a new one, and sets new rice in it with a new straw cap, and it is cold for a whole year. Then, one morning in the tenth month, a little warm. You did not mean to. Some things do not stay let go.

events.text: The crossroads has become a market. Every fifth day the five roads bring it in: salt from the coast, cloth from the weavers' villages, cattle from the hills, pots, knives, straw shoes, dried fish, medicine roots. By noon there are three thousand feet on you, haggling. By dusk the place is empty and swept, and you lie under the litter of the day, counting it.

choices.text: Learn every voice in it

effects.log: The salt-seller who lies about the weight and the cloth-seller who lies about the weave. The cattle dealer who never lies, and charges for it. The old woman with medicine roots who knows more than the county doctor. In a year you know them all. In two you know their children.

choices.text: Keep the ground dry and firm on market days

effects.log: It never rains hard on a market day. Or it does, and the market ground drains in an hour. The traders begin to say this is the luckiest market in the province. It brings more traders. (Earth +1)

choices.text: Feel what the whole market weighs

effects.log: Salt and cloth and cattle and coin, and more than that: debts, bargains, quarrels, a match between two families settled over a bowl of soup. A market is heavier than a crossroads. It is not only the things. It is all the agreeing.

events.text: A bull at the cattle pens breaks its rope and goes through the market at a run, head down, through the pottery, through the cloth, toward the place where the children are watching a puppet show.

choices.text: Open a soft rut in front of it

effects.log: The ground goes soft as a paddy under the bull's front hooves, ten paces from the children. It goes down on its knees in the mud, astonished, and sits there blowing until its owner comes. The puppeteer never finishes the show. Nobody cares.

choices.text: Make the ground tremble so the crowd scatters

ok.log: Everyone runs at once, the children too, in every direction, which is exactly right. The bull goes through an empty space and into the river, and stands there cooling off and looking embarrassed.

fail.log: Everyone runs, and some run the wrong way. A pot-seller's stall goes over and a boy breaks an arm. The bull is caught at the river. It could have been worse. You feel every broken pot in your middle. (-4 health)

choices.text: Calm the bull through its hooves

effects.log: Warmth comes up through four hooves into a very frightened animal. It slows. It stops. It stands in the middle of the cloth stalls breathing hard, and then lowers its head and eats a bolt of green hemp. The cloth-seller wants compensation. That is a different story.

events.text: The rice-cake seller and the knife-grinder have fought for eleven market days over the same patch of ground: the exact middle of the market, where the five roads meet, where everybody passes and everybody stops. Both of them say it is lucky. Both of them are right.

choices.text: Make the middle too warm to sit on

effects.log: The ground is warm as a bathhouse floor in the exact middle. Neither of them can bear to sit there for long. In the end they set up on either side of the warm patch and glare at each other across it, and everyone walks through the middle between them, and both do very well.

choices.text: Favour the rice cakes: food before knives

effects.log: The knife-grinder's wheel will not turn on that spot, however much grease. The rice-cake seller sets up in triumph. The knife-grinder moves to the county road and does better there. Nobody quite knows why. (Earth +1)

choices.text: Favour the knives: a market needs edges

effects.log: The rice cakes go stale on the middle patch, every time. The grinder sets up there, sparks flying, and every farmer brings a sickle. The rice-cake seller moves to the grave road and sells to mourners, who are always hungry. (Metal +1)

events.text: A typhoon on a market day. The sky goes yellow at noon and the wind comes in off the sea, and three thousand people are caught in the open with their cattle and their cloth and their children. The stalls begin to go.

choices.text: Hold the whole market down

ok.log: The wind takes every roof in the county and not one stall in the market. People lie flat on the warm ground and hold on to it, and it holds on to them. Afterwards they come out and look at each other and do not quite say it.

fail.log: You hold the middle. The edges go: awnings, baskets, a cow tumbling over and over into the ditch, unhurt and furious. Nobody dies. You lie exhausted under the ruin of the day. (-8 health)

choices.text: Open the cellars and the ditches for them to shelter

effects.log: The ground opens a little everywhere, the drains and the root cellars and the old ditches, deep and dry. People crawl into them with their children and their goods. The stalls blow away. The people do not.

events.text: The market has become a town. Tiled roofs round the square, a permanent inn, a drum tower that beats the five-day rhythm. The county has noticed and sent a clerk with a ledger. The five roads are paved for a mile out with flat stones. Every stone is set into you.

choices.text: Bear the stones gladly

effects.log: A town is heavier than a market. You take every paving stone and every roof-beam and the drum tower's foundation, and settle under them, and find you can. It is the first time you think: I could carry a great deal. It is not quite a happy thought.

choices.text: Keep one patch of the old earth bare in the middle

effects.log: They pave the whole square except the middle, where the stones will not lie flat, however often they are reset. In the end they leave it bare, and put the cairn back there. A town with a patch of dirt at its heart. It suits you.

events.text: {npc}, the biggest rice merchant in the market, has two sets of weights: a heavy set for buying and a light set for selling. Today an old widow from the hills brings in a whole year's rice to sell, and {npc} weighs it with the heavy ones. Half a year of work is gone in a breath, and the widow does not know it.

choices.text: Make the false weight show itself

effects.log: The iron weight on the beam slides of its own accord, a full notch, in front of the queue. A peddler sees it. Then everyone sees it. {npc} goes the colour of old rice and weighs it again, honestly, in silence. (Metal +1)

choices.text: Send the widow a stranger who knows weights

effects.log: A travelling grain clerk, passing through, stops beside the scale and looks at the weights and says, mildly, that those are not county weights. The widow gets the full price. {npc} gets a look from the clerk that lasts the rest of the year.

choices.text: Watch, and learn how cheating feels from below

effects.log: It feels like a stone in your sandal, a tiny wrongness that the whole market stands on. You learn what it is today. You will feel it in every market and every county and every kingdom you ever lie under.

events.text: {npc} has new weights, and they are honest, and {npc} hates every one of them. Now {npc} wets the rice before selling it so it weighs more, and cuts the cloth a finger short. There are a hundred ways to cheat that do not involve a scale.

choices.text: Dry the rice in the sacks overnight

effects.log: Every sack that {npc} wets is bone-dry by morning, however much water went in. The merchant stands over them, damp to the elbows, and begins to suspect the market itself. Correctly. (Earth +1)

choices.text: Let it go. You cannot watch every sack

effects.log: You cannot. That is the second lesson. A centre that tries to catch every cheat in a market becomes a market inspector, and a market inspector is not a dragon. You let the small cheats be small. You watch the big ones.

choices.text: Give {npc} one honest year of very good business

effects.log: An honest year, and somehow the best year {npc} has ever had: more customers, better rice, a new storehouse. {npc} does not understand it. {npc} does not cheat again, out of superstition. You will take superstition.

events.text: The county sends a market inspector with a set of standard measures in a locked box, a ladle and a peck and a steelyard, and a seal. The inspector is to make every measure in the market match the box. The inspector is also, you can feel at once, open to small gifts.

choices.text: Make the inspector's own measures true

effects.log: The box measures are a little false themselves, and the inspector knows it. By the end of the visit they are not, and the inspector does not know how. The whole market is measured against a true standard for the first time in its life. (Metal +1, Earth +1)

choices.text: Let the inspector take the gifts and do the work anyway

effects.log: The gifts go into a sleeve. The measures still come out right, because you keep the beam steady through the whole inspection. The inspector goes home richer and honest by accident. You learn that rule can work through crooked people. It is not a comfortable lesson.

choices.text: Shame the inspector in front of the market

effects.log: The locked box falls open in the middle of the square, and the seal rolls out, and so does a purse that is not the county's. The inspector is recalled. The next inspector is very, very honest and very slow. Fear works. It is slow.

events.text: {npc} is old, and the business has gone to {his} child, who weighs everything twice and gives a handful over. The old merchant sits at the edge of the market in the sun, watching the scale, and one day says to nobody in particular: it was the ground. I always knew it was the ground.

choices.text: Warm the ground under the old merchant

effects.npcPass: old age, in the sun at the edge of the market

mem.note: warmed the market ground for me at the end

effects.log: {npc} feels it, and laughs, a dry old laugh, and puts a palm on the stones. That winter {npc} dies, and the child puts a small honest weight in the coffin. You think that is the right joke.

choices.text: Stay cool. Some things are not forgiven by being warm

effects.log: Nothing. {npc} sits in the sun a while, nods as if the ground had answered anyway, and goes home. The widow from the hills died poor. You have not forgotten.

events.text: There is a saying in the province now: honest as the scales at the crossroads market. Merchants from three counties bring their weights to be tried there. A stone weight with a dragon carved on it hangs on a post in the middle of the square, and nobody remembers who made it.

choices.text: Keep the saying true

effects.log: Year after year, every weight tried there comes out true or comes out shamed. The saying goes into the songs. Somebody, generations from now, will buy a scale in this market and be astonished that it is honest. You will be gone by then. The scale will not.

choices.text: Let the town keep it true without you

effects.log: You stop watching the scale, a little at a time, to see what happens. Nothing happens. The town does it now. The merchants watch each other. It is the first thing you have ever given away that kept working.

events.text: Another market day, another thumb on a scale: a salt-seller who has found a new way to make a peck hold less. It is small. It is always small. The whole market stands on a thousand small things like it.

choices.text: Make the peck true again, quietly

effects.log: The peck holds a peck. The salt-seller frowns at it for a week, then shrugs. The farmers go home with the salt they paid for, and never know it was ever otherwise. (Metal +1)

choices.text: Let the salt spill in front of everyone

effects.log: The false bottom of the peck gives way in the middle of a sale. Salt everywhere, and a hollow where there should not be one. The queue goes very quiet. The salt-seller packs up early that day, and the next.

choices.text: Let this one go

effects.log: Not every cheat is yours to catch. Somebody in the queue notices, and says so, loudly, and the salt-seller blusters and gives a handful over. The market can do it too. Good.

events.text: The first full moon, and the farmers' band comes down to the crossroads now, not to one yard: the little gong, the hourglass drum, the barrel drum, the big gong, and the whole village dancing behind. They stamp in a ring round the cairn and sing to the earth to stay quiet and kind for another year.
events.arc: The Band at the First Full Moon

choices.text: Stamp back, once, under the whole ring

effects.log: Once, from below, under two hundred feet. The ring stops dead. Then the little gong starts again, twice as fast, and the dancing goes on until dawn, wilder than anyone can remember.

choices.text: Lie quiet and kind, as they ask

effects.log: They ask the earth to be still, and you are still. It is an odd thing to be begged for, and an easy thing to give. The year is a quiet one, as asked.

choices.text: Warm the ground for the dancers' bare feet

effects.log: The frozen crossroads goes soft and warm under the dancing. Nobody's feet hurt that night. The old drummer says it is the best ground in the county for stamping, and means it as high praise.

events.text: The peddlers follow the five-day markets round the province on foot: the pack-peddlers with cloth and ginseng and brass on their backs, the frame-peddlers with pots and salt and dried fish on wooden carrying frames. Their old headman stops at the market cairn and lays a coin on it, and asks the ground, out loud, for safe roads.

choices.text: Give them safe roads

effects.log: No robbers on any road that leads to your market, all year. The peddlers notice before anyone else does. They notice everything. By the next season every peddler in the province stops at your cairn.

choices.text: Ask what they carry besides goods

effects.log: News. Letters. Marriages arranged between markets ten days apart. Medicine. Rumours of war. Songs. The peddlers are the roads walking. You decide, listening, that they are a kind of crossroads too, a moving one.

events.text: {npc} is a young frame-peddler who has decided the market cairn is lucky. Every fifth day, every market, {npc} stops and lays a pebble and asks for luck. It has been going on for years. It is going to go on, you begin to suspect, for decades.

choices.text: Answer every time, a little

mem.note: always answered me at the market cairn

effects.log: A small luck every fifth day: a sale, a dry road, a lost knife found. Nothing that makes {npc} rich. Everything that makes {npc} keep walking. Years of it, very small, add up to a life.

choices.text: Answer once, big, and see what happens

effects.log: A whole cartload of brassware, abandoned by a frightened merchant on the hill road, waiting for {npc}. {npc} is rich for a year, and then not, and is back at the cairn the next fifth day with a pebble. Big luck does not change a peddler. Small luck is what they live on.

events.text: The peddlers have a guild now, with a headquarters in the market town, a seal, rules, a fund for funerals, and rods for punishing members who cheat. The county uses them to carry messages in a crisis. They are proud, and useful, and growing. Today their headmen are deciding that only guild members may sell in your market.

choices.text: Let the rule stand. Order is good for a market

effects.log: The guild runs the market from that year on. It is honest, mostly, and orderly, and closed. The old woman with the medicine roots is turned away. You feel the market grow heavier and stiffer, like a field trodden flat. (Metal +1)

choices.text: Make the market ground refuse the rule

effects.log: The guild's rods split in the rain. Their stalls lean. Every outsider who sets up on the edge of the market has a remarkable day. The headmen, who are not fools, take the rule back after a year and call it their own generosity.

choices.text: Send the old headman a dream of the first coin on the cairn

effects.log: The old headman remembers walking these roads with nothing, asking the ground for luck. At the next meeting the old one stands up and says so. The rule fails by one voice.

events.text: {npc} is old and bent under the carrying frame, and comes to the cairn for the last time with a pebble from every market in the province, a whole bagful, forty years of fifth days. {npc} pours them out on the cairn one by one, naming each market, and asks for nothing.

choices.text: Thank {him}, through the warm stones

effects.npcPass: old age, at home, the carrying frame by the door
effects.log: Every pebble is warm as {npc} lays it down. {npc} notices on the third, and goes very slowly through the rest. At the end {npc} bows to the cairn as to an old partner, and walks home, and does not walk the roads again.

choices.text: Keep one pebble at your middle

effects.npcPass: old age, in a market inn
effects.log: One pebble from the river market sinks into the ground under the cairn and is not found again. It is the one {npc} named last. You keep it. It is a very small weight, and you are glad of it.

events.text: A fever comes in with a load of cloth from the coast. It goes out again with every peddler, every buyer, every cart. In a week it is in eleven villages. A centre gathers things in from five roads; it sends them out again just as fast. This is one of them.

choices.text: Close the roads: make every one a mire

effects.log: All five roads go to deep mud overnight, in a dry month. Nobody can come and nobody can go. The market dies for a season. The fever stops at the edge of the town. Hungry is better than dead, the herb-seller says. The salt-sellers do not agree.

choices.text: Let the market run, and hold the sick up

ok.log: You spend the whole season pushing warmth up into every sickbed in the town. Fewer die than anyone can explain. You are thin and cold by the end of it. (-4 health)

fail.log: There are too many beds. You hold up what you can and feel the rest go. It is the first time you understand that a centre cannot hold up everything, and that it is going to keep trying. (-10 health)

choices.text: Draw the herb-seller to the right root

effects.log: A root that the old herb-seller never noticed in twenty years is suddenly everywhere at the edge of the market road, pushing up through the dust. The herb-seller tries it. It works. The fever passes in a month.

events.text: After the fever, the town burns the cloth that brought it, in a great smoky heap in the square, and then argues for a month about who should pay the cloth merchants. The cloth merchants want the town to pay. The town wants the coast to pay. The coast is a long way off.

choices.text: Warm the ashes into good soil for the poorest field

effects.log: The ash goes on a widow's field outside the town and the next year's cabbages are the size of drums. It does not settle the argument. It does feed somebody. (Wood +1)

choices.text: Let them argue; it is theirs to settle

effects.log: They argue for a whole year and settle in the end by splitting it three ways, which satisfies nobody, which is how you know it is fair. You did nothing. It took them a year. It would have taken you an afternoon. You begin to see why that is not the point.

events.text: Years later a new cloth ship comes up from the coast, and the town will not let it unload. The captain swears the crew is healthy. The town remembers. A centre has a long memory and a short temper about the same thing twice.

choices.text: Tell the town, in the ground, that the ship is clean

effects.log: The ground under the quay is warm and easy, and somehow the town feels it. They unload, nervously, and nobody falls sick. The market has its cloth again, and a long memory that has learned one exception.

choices.text: Let them be careful

effects.log: The ship waits a month at anchor while the town makes up its mind. Nobody falls sick. The captain is furious. The town feels safe. Both are right, which is the trouble with being a centre.

events.text: Bandits have found the crossroads. It is the best place in the county to rob anybody: five roads to come from, five roads to escape by, and every cart has to pass through the middle. Tonight they have a salt merchant's cart stopped right over you.

choices.text: Throw the bandits off their feet

ok.log: The ground bucks under them like a startled horse. Clubs fly. The bandits scatter down four different roads and the salt merchant down the fifth. The crossroads is quiet before the dust settles.

fail.log: The ground bucks, and the cart goes over, and a bandit with a spear stabs at the earth in a panic and finds you. It is a small wound in a large body. They get away with half the salt. (-8 health)

choices.text: Close four roads and leave them only the road to the county jail

effects.log: Four roads go soft as rice porridge under their feet. The fifth is firm and dry and leads, in a mile, straight to the guardhouse. They run down it in the dark. The guards cannot believe their luck.

choices.text: Let the salt go and keep the merchant safe

effects.log: You hold the ground still under the merchant and let the bandits take what they came for. Nobody is hurt. Salt can be bought again. The merchant does not think so, loudly, all the way home.

events.text: The bandits' chief has noticed that the crossroads fights back. {npc} comes alone at midnight to the cairn, sits down, and talks to it like a rival: you cost me two good men and a winter's salt. What do you want? Nobody else talks to the ground. {npc} has guessed.

choices.text: Make the cairn warm, and wait

effects.log: {npc} feels it, and goes very still. Then {npc} talks all night: a burned village, a debt, a magistrate. In the morning {npc} goes away up the hill road, and the robberies stop for a whole year. Nobody tells the village why.

choices.text: Shake the cairn down on {npc}'s feet

effects.log: The stones come down. {npc} jumps clear, laughing, a little wildly, and says: so that is a no. The band moves to the next county. They are robbing somebody else now. That is not quite the same as stopping.

events.text: The old bandit chief has come back, grey, without a band, and taken a job as the crossroads guard. {npc} sleeps on duty sometimes, right over you, the way an old guard once did. The village has no idea. Some nights {npc} sits up and tells the cairn who is coming down which road, before they come.

choices.text: Keep the old guard company

effects.npcPass: old age, asleep at the crossroads
effects.log: Years of it. Nobody is robbed. When {npc} dies, asleep on the warm ground one autumn night, the village buries the old guard by the cairn and never learns whose bones they are honouring. You do not tell them. It is a good grave.

choices.text: Let {npc} be a guard, and nothing more

effects.log: You give no sign. {npc} guards the crossroads well, the way only an old thief can, and teaches the young guards which bushes to watch. The county has never had such a safe road and does not know why.

events.text: Robbers on the roads again, as there always are where roads meet. A new band this time, young and hungry, waiting in the ditch by the market road for the evening carts.

choices.text: Turn the ditch to mud under them

ok.log: The ditch fills with warm mud to the waist in a breath. The robbers flounder out, robbed of their dignity, and the carts go by laughing. The band breaks up that season.

fail.log: The mud comes too slowly and they are out and onto the road. A carter loses a purse and a tooth. You feel the purse more than the tooth, oddly. (-5 health)

choices.text: Warn the carters with a tremor

effects.log: The road shivers under the first ox, and the ox stops and will not go on, and the carters look about and see the shapes in the ditch. They go round by the river road. Nobody is robbed tonight.

choices.text: Let the county guard deal with it

effects.log: You leave it. Some nights the guards are there and some nights not. A centre that rescues every cart becomes a cart-guard. You are learning, slowly and not happily, what not to carry.

events.text: The town is a county seat now, and the county has a yamen built over you: a gate, a courtyard, a hall with a tiled roof, and a desk. At the desk sits {npc}, the new magistrate, three months in office. Every decision {npc} makes, you feel: a tax, a sentence, a refusal, a pardon, each one set down on your back like a sack.

choices.text: Bear it, and learn what each one weighs

effects.log: A flogging weighs more than a fine. A pardon weighs nearly nothing, and a wrong pardon weighs more than anything. A tax in a bad year is a millstone. You learn the scale of it. You will carry it for the rest of your life, in larger and larger sizes. (Weight +2)

choices.text: Shift under the hall, so {npc} feels it too

effects.log: The desk creaks. The floor tilts a hair. {npc} looks up from the papers and frowns at the floor for a long time, and the next sentence {npc} gives is lighter. You have discovered that a ruler can be made to feel the ground.

choices.text: Lie still and see what kind of magistrate this is

effects.log: You give no sign. You watch. A ruler who does not know the ground is listening is a ruler you can know truly. In a month you know {npc} better than {npc}'s own family does.

events.text: A test, though {npc} does not know it is one. A rich landowner and a tenant farmer come to the yamen over the same paddy. The landowner has a deed, freshly written. The tenant has forty years of working it, and a grandfather who cleared it. A silver ingot has already changed hands, in a sleeve, in the corridor.

choices.text: Send {npc} a dream of the paddy being cleared

effects.log: That night {npc} dreams of a young farmer with an axe and a field of stumps, sweating, forty years ago. In the morning {npc} sends the silver back, rules for the tenant, and looks as if no sleep was had at all. (Weight +1)

choices.text: Let {npc} choose freely, and remember it

ok.log: {npc} rules for the tenant, and returns the silver, without any help from you. You feel the weight of it settle on your back and find it is light. An honest ruler is the lightest thing to carry. You did not know that.

fail.log: {npc} rules for the landowner and keeps the silver. The tenant walks out of the yamen gate past the place you lie, and the ruling sits on you like a cold stone all winter. (Weight +4)

choices.text: Make the forged deed's ink run in front of the court

effects.log: The ink of the new deed runs down the paper in a warm damp morning like tears. Everybody in the court sees it. {npc} has no choice. The tenant keeps the paddy. {npc} is uneasy in that hall ever after, which is not a bad thing for a magistrate. (Weight +1)

events.text: {npc} has a new rice measure made for the county tax: the same size outside as the old one, a finger deeper inside. The county will pay a tenth more and never see it. It is a very clever measure, and every farmer who pours rice into it pours a little of themselves onto your back.

choices.text: Crack the new measure on the first day

effects.log: It splits along the false bottom the first time it is filled, in the yamen courtyard, in front of a queue of farmers. The old measure comes back out of the storehouse. {npc} blames the carpenter. Everybody knows. (Metal +1, Weight -2)

choices.text: Make {npc} carry a sack of tax rice to the granary personally

effects.log: A clerk falls ill, and another, and on the third day {npc} ends up carrying sacks in the courtyard in an official robe, cursing. By evening {npc} knows exactly what a tenth more weighs. The measure quietly disappears.

choices.text: Bear it, and wait

effects.log: A tenth more, every autumn, on your back. You learn the exact weight of a small greed repeated a thousand times. It is heavier than a large one. (Weight +3)

events.text: {npc}, the captain of the yamen guard, stands alone in the empty courtyard after midnight and asks the ground a question nobody has asked it before: whose county is this, really? The magistrate's? The king's? The farmers'? The captain has been thinking about it for a long time, standing guard on top of you.

choices.text: Warm the stones under the captain's feet

mem.note: warmed the yamen courtyard when I asked

effects.log: No answer, only warmth. {npc} stands in it a long time and then laughs quietly and says: the ground's, then. Of course. {npc} guards the yamen differently after that, as if guarding something under it.

choices.text: Shake the gate, once: not yours to ask

effects.log: The great gate bangs in the windless night. {npc} jumps, and bows to nothing, and goes back to the guardroom. A good soldier knows when a question has been refused. You are not sure you were right to refuse it.

choices.text: Answer in a dream: whoever is standing on it

effects.log: In the dream {npc} stands on the yamen roof and sees the whole county, and every farmer in it standing on their own field. Whoever is standing on it. {npc} wakes puzzled, and is kinder to the farmers at the gate from then on.

events.text: A famine year. {npc} sits in the yamen at night with the county granary ledger and the relief orders from the capital and a list of villages, and has to choose which villages get rice first. Each name {npc} writes goes straight down onto your back. It is the heaviest night you have ever felt.

choices.text: Carry it all yourself, without a sign

effects.log: You hold every name. {npc} writes until dawn and never knows that the ground under the desk was holding up the choosing. The relief goes out. You lie under the yamen for a month after, unable to move. (Weight +5)

choices.text: Let {npc} feel how heavy it is, and share it with the village heads

effects.log: The ledger gets heavier and heavier in {npc}'s hands until {npc} puts it down and sends for the village heads instead, all eleven, and they choose together through the night, arguing. They choose better than {npc} would have. You feel the weight spread out across the county like rain on a field. (Weight -4)

choices.text: Make the granary find a forgotten store

ok.log: A clerk, sent to count the empty bins again, finds a sealed room nobody has opened in thirty years, full of old rice, dry and sound. Every village gets something. The choosing is still hard. It is less hard.

fail.log: The forgotten store is there, but the rats found it first. Nothing in it but husks. {npc} chooses alone after all, by candlelight, and you carry every name. (Weight +3)

events.text: {npc}'s term is over. The magistrate is going back to the capital with a cartload of books and less silver than anyone expected. The county is arguing about whether to raise a stone tablet at the yamen gate, carved with the magistrate's name and the words good government. Some want it. Some would rather throw stones at it.

choices.text: Let the tablet stand, if the county wants it

effects.log: The tablet goes up at the gate, and you take its foot firmly into the ground. When the magistrate's cart rolls past it, {npc} looks at it and does not quite smile. The weight of all those years lifts off your back as the cart goes, all at once, like a load set down. (Weight -3)

choices.text: Tilt the tablet, a little, so nobody forgets

effects.log: It leans. However often they straighten it, it leans. In a hundred years it is a famous leaning tablet, and children ask why, and the old people say: because nobody is all good. That is true of everybody. You leave it leaning. (Weight -2)

choices.text: Let the cart go, and keep the years

effects.log: The magistrate goes. The decisions do not. Every ruling of those years is still on your back, and you find you do not know how to put them down. Somebody new is already unpacking at the desk. (Weight +1)

events.text: Under the great zelkova at the edge of the square the village elders meet, as they have met for three hundred years: seven old people on straw mats with long pipes, deciding the things the magistrate never hears about. Today it is water: whose paddy gets the stream first in a dry spring. You know the right answer. You could make it happen tonight.

choices.text: Give it to the elders, and let them decide

effects.log: You do nothing. They argue for three days, smoke a great deal, and decide on a turn-by-turn order that is not quite what you would have done. It is theirs. You feel the water question go off your back and onto seven bent ones, which are used to it. (Weight -4)

choices.text: Decide it yourself, quietly, with the stream

effects.log: The stream finds its own way, at night, to the right paddies in the right order. The elders arrive at the meeting to find it already settled and are relieved and a little hurt. You carry the water now. (Weight +2, Water +1)

events.text: The elders decide badly. A dispute over a boundary stone, and they give it to the family with the most sons, as elders sometimes do. A widow loses a strip of field. You could undo it. You gave them the deciding.

choices.text: Leave it decided

effects.log: It is wrong, and you leave it, and it is the hardest thing you have done under this village. Next year one of the elders, without knowing why, gives the widow a strip of his own. The village is lumpy and unfair and alive. (Weight -2)

choices.text: Move the boundary stone back in the night

effects.log: The stone is back where it was by morning. The family with the sons accuses the widow. The elders accuse each other. Nobody trusts the stones now. You have taken the deciding back, and its weight with it. (Weight +3)

events.text: The elders have been deciding for years now, things you once would have done yourself: water, boundaries, the timing of the harvest, who marries whom across the stream. They are good at it. Better than they were. One of them sits down on the root of the zelkova one evening and says: it is as if somebody is listening.

choices.text: Warm the root, to say you are

effects.log: The root is warm. The old one keeps a hand on it a long time, and tells nobody, and is very slightly kinder in every decision after. The weight of all that deciding sits on the zelkova now, and the zelkova is very old and does not mind. (Weight -2)

choices.text: Stay cool: let them think they are alone

effects.log: Nobody is listening, the old one decides, and goes on deciding well anyway. That is the point. You feel lighter than you have since the yamen was built. (Weight -3)

events.text: The zelkova is dying. Five hundred years old, hollow, struck by lightning twice, and this spring only one branch leafs. The elders sit under it anyway. They are talking about whether to cut it down and plant a new one, and where the meetings will be held for the hundred years it takes to grow.

choices.text: Pour your warmth into the old roots

effects.log: All spring and summer, warmth up into dead wood. In autumn three more branches have leaves. It will live another sixty years. It costs you more than you expected, and you would do it again. (Wood +2, -5 health)

choices.text: Let it go, and warm the seedling instead

effects.log: They plant a seedling beside it and the old tree comes down in the winter. The elders meet under the stump and a sapling, in the sun, grumbling. It will take a hundred years. You have a hundred years. (Wood +1)

events.text: Earth dams water, and the earth is you. You have grown too strong, too heavy, too full, and the water of the valley has nowhere to go. The wells go dry one by one, from the yamen well outwards. The paddies crack. The rice stands brown in them. It is not a curse. It is only you.

choices.text: Lie still and feel every dry well

effects.log: Every one. The village well, the temple well, the deep well at the inn. Every bucket that comes up empty. You do not look away. If this is what too much of you does, you mean to know its exact shape.

choices.text: Loosen your hold on the deep water

effects.log: You make yourself smaller, softer, as far down as you can reach. It hurts the way unclenching a cramped hand hurts. By autumn three wells have a little water in the bottom. It is not enough. It is a start. (-6 health)

choices.text: Send the people to the river with buckets

effects.log: The road to the river is firm and smooth all summer, for the first time anyone can remember. A line of people with buckets walks it every day from dawn. The rice is lost. The people are not.

events.text: The drought year is over, but the people remember. The county shaman holds a rain rite at the river, with a dragon painted on a great sheet of paper hung from a pole, and a pig, and drums. The rite is to beg the dragon to give back the water. You are the dragon, in a way. Just not the one they painted.

choices.text: Give back the water: earth yields to water

effects.log: You let go, deliberately, the way you never have, and the water you had been damming without meaning to runs on into the wells. Earth shrinks. Water swells. The rite is declared a great success. (Earth -2, Water +2)

choices.text: Watch the rite, and learn what they think a dragon is

effects.log: A dragon, they think, is something in the sky that has the rain and will not give it. They are half right. The painted dragon on the paper is blue. You are not offended. You are taking notes.

events.text: A warning year. The wells are not dry, not yet, but they are lower than they were, and the old well-digger at the inn says the water tastes of clay. You can feel why. You are a little too much this year: too heavy, too warm, too full of yourself.

choices.text: Stop growing for a season

effects.log: You do not settle. You do not feed. You lie as light as you can, all season, and the wells come up a finger, and the water tastes of water again. (Earth -2, Water +1)

choices.text: Give the extra to the forges: earth bears metal

effects.log: The smithies have a good year: iron ore turns up in a farmer's ditch, and the hill forge has fuel to spare. The wells come back. Somewhere, something metal grows a little sharper. (Earth -2, Metal +2)

choices.text: Ignore it. It is a good harvest

effects.log: It is a very good harvest. The wells go a little lower. The old well-digger says nothing, because nobody asks. (Earth +1)

events.text: Years after the drought, the old well at the inn has water in it again, sweet and cold. The innkeeper's grandson lowers a bucket and drinks and says it is the best water in the county. It is. You let it through on purpose now.

choices.text: Keep it sweet

effects.log: Every bucket, sweet and cold. You keep a channel open through yourself all the time now, a little looseness at your middle where the water goes by. It is a small discomfort. You have stopped minding it. (Water +1)

choices.text: Remember why it was dry

effects.log: You remember. You will need to remember this later, when you are a great deal bigger and a great deal more full of yourself. Earth dams water. You are earth.

events.text: Water quenches fire. The summer does not come. It rains in the fifth month and the sixth and the seventh, cold, steady, endless. Hearths will not stay lit. The rice stays green in the paddies and never fills. The children are coughing, and there is no dry wood anywhere.

choices.text: Hold what warmth you have under the houses

effects.log: You give your heat up through every floor in the village, all summer, the way you once warmed a single jar. The children stop coughing. The rice still does not ripen. You are cold to your middle by autumn. (-6 health)

choices.text: Drink the rain as fast as it falls

effects.log: You take the water down as fast as it comes, and the paddies drain, and the floors are dry. It is not enough to make the summer come. It is enough that the houses do not rot. Some rice is saved.

choices.text: Show the farmers which slopes still get the sun

effects.log: One south slope, one sheltered terrace, one corner of a field by the warm wall of the yamen: the ground there is drier and the rice does fill, a little. The farmers find it by the colour. It is a hungry winter. Not a starving one.

events.text: The winter after the cold summer. The granaries are half empty. The magistrate's relief rice is late. In the market the price of a peck has tripled, and the peddlers are not coming, because nobody has anything to buy with.

choices.text: Warm the seed-rice so it keeps through the spring

effects.log: Whatever else gets eaten, the seed-rice in every house stays dry and sound and warm. In the spring there is something to plant. A hungry year does not become two. (Fire +1)

choices.text: Bring the summer back gently next year

effects.log: In the eighteen days before summer you hold the hand-over carefully, and the next summer comes in hot and early and whole. The rice ripens a week ahead. (Water -2, Fire +2)

events.text: A warning year: too much rain in spring, and it does not want to stop. The river is high and grey and the frogs are loud in the paddies all day. Water is swelling. Fire, the summer, is waiting at the door for its turn and cannot get in.

choices.text: Turn the rain toward the woods: water feeds wood

effects.log: The rain goes into the hills and the forests drink it, and the bamboo grows like a song. The paddies drain. Summer gets in the door on time. (Water -2, Wood +2)

choices.text: Let it rain

effects.log: It rains, and you drink, and grow a little softer. Summer comes late and thin. Nothing bad happens this year. (Water +1)

events.text: Metal cuts wood. The forge town up the river has grown too hungry: swords for the garrison, ploughshares, iron pots, nails for the yamen roof. It needs charcoal, and charcoal needs trees, and the hills behind the town are bare to the ridge. In the summer rains the slopes come down.

choices.text: Hold the bare slopes with your own strength

effects.log: You grip the hillside from beneath, the way roots should have. Two slopes stay. One comes down on an empty field. Nobody dies. You lie under the hills all summer with your grip locked, aching. (-5 health)

choices.text: Warn the valley farms with a tremor before each slide

effects.log: Every time a slope is about to go, the ground under the farms below it trembles first, a long low shiver. The farmers learn to run. The houses go. The people do not.

events.text: The forge town has sent a man up into the bare hills with a sack of pine seedlings. One man, one sack. The slope is a mile wide. It would take a lifetime.

choices.text: Warm every seedling the man plants

effects.log: Every one takes. The man comes back with another sack, and then the town sends three more men, because it is working. In a few years the slope is a young forest. (Wood +2)

choices.text: Let the forges cool a little, to give the trees time

effects.log: Ore is harder to find for a few years, the seams thinner, the iron poorer. The forges slow. The hills breathe. Metal gathers water: the springs on the bare slopes start up again. (Metal -2, Water +1)

events.text: A warning year: the garrison has doubled, and every forge in the county is working day and night. The smoke hangs over the river. Somebody is preparing for a war that has not been announced. The hills are thinning.

choices.text: Let the metal cool into water

effects.log: A wet autumn, and every blade in the garrison rusts at the edge. The quartermaster is furious. The hills keep their trees another year. (Metal -2, Water +2)

choices.text: Let them arm. A county must defend itself

effects.log: The forges roar all winter. The garrison is the best armed in the province. The hills behind the forge town are bare to the ridge. (Metal +2)

events.text: Wood breaks earth, and earth is you. A spring too strong for too long, and the roots have got into everything: the terrace walls, the paddy dykes, the foundations of the yamen. In the summer rains the terraces split along the roots and whole fields slide downhill, rice and all. You feel it as a tearing at your edges.

choices.text: Hold the terraces together from beneath

ok.log: You pull the cracked walls back together like the edges of a wound and hold them all summer. Two fields are lost. Thirty are saved. The farmers say the terraces were built by their great-grandfathers, and are proud of them.

fail.log: You hold, and the roots are stronger. Field after field goes downhill. You are torn at the edges for a year, like a coat at the seams. (-8 health)

choices.text: Let the fields go and keep the houses

effects.log: You put everything you have under the village and nothing under the fields. Five fields slide. Not one house cracks. The farmers rebuild terraces all winter. They are alive to do it.

events.text: After the slides, the farmers rebuild the terraces with stone, and the magistrate sends woodcutters into the thickets along the dykes. A whole hillside of young trees is coming down.

choices.text: Let the woodcutters cut: wood feeds fire

effects.log: The wood goes to the hearths and the kilns, and the winter is warm, and the pottery of the county has a famous year. The terraces hold. (Wood -2, Fire +2)

choices.text: Ask the roots to go down, not sideways

effects.log: It takes years of patience, warm below and cool above, coaxing. The roots learn. The terraces hold without the hillside being stripped. You are proud of this one. (Wood -1, Earth +1)

events.text: A warning year: the bamboo is coming up through the floor of the yamen storehouse, and the willows along the stream have doubled. Spring will not hand over to summer. Wood is pushing everything.

choices.text: Feed the push into the summer

effects.log: Wood feeds fire. The summer arrives in a rush, hot and early, and the bamboo browns at the tips and stops. (Wood -2, Fire +2)

choices.text: Hold the line under the storehouse

effects.log: The bamboo stops at the floor. It goes sideways along under the boards, sulking, all summer. Nothing is broken. Nothing is settled either. (Wood -1)

events.text: Fire melts metal. A summer of fires: a dry wind, a careless lamp, and the county armoury goes up in a night, every spear and helmet in it running red and soft. The granary beside it catches. The harvest goes up with it.

choices.text: Open the ground under the granary, to save the grain

effects.log: The granary floor sags and splits, and half the rice pours down into a cool cavern in the clay, out of the fire. The roof falls in on empty bins. In the morning they dig the rice out, smoky and sound.

choices.text: Smother the fire with dust

ok.log: A wall of yellow dust comes up off the whole square and down on the fire like a blanket. The armoury is lost. The granary is singed. The town is saved.

fail.log: The dust comes up and the wind takes it the wrong way. The granary burns. You lie under the ash all night, feeling every coal. (-7 health)

events.text: The smiths are trying to recast the spears from the melted lumps of the old armoury. It is not going well. The iron is burnt and brittle, and the garrison commander is shouting.

choices.text: Cool the forge-water: let metal come back

effects.log: The quench is cold and clean every time, and the spears come out true. The commander stops shouting. The summer finally cools. (Fire -2, Metal +2)

choices.text: Let the spears stay broken

effects.log: The garrison has no spears for a year. Nothing happens. The commander discovers that a county can go a year without spears. You file it away.

events.text: A warning year: a hot dry summer, and three fires already in the market town, small ones. The thatch is like tinder. Fire is waxing. Metal, autumn, is far away.

choices.text: Draw the heat down into yourself: fire makes earth

effects.log: You drink the heat out of the ground of the town all summer. The fires stop. You are very warm, and a little bigger. (Fire -2, Earth +1)

choices.text: Let the summer burn

effects.log: A hot, golden summer and a great melon harvest. Two more small fires. The town is careful with its lamps. (Fire +1)

events.text: Weather over the ridge, and not the ordinary kind. A young dragon of the east has grown up in the pool of the next valley, green-blue, proud, all rain and spring, and it has felt you: something large and old and warm lying under a crossroads where it thinks a dragon ought not to be. It sends a storm over the ridge, as a challenge.
events.arc: The Dragon of the Next Valley

choices.text: Answer with stillness

effects.log: You lie still under the storm and let it rain. Earth does not move. The young one in the next valley is baffled, and then furious, and sends a bigger storm. You drink it. This could go on a long time.

choices.text: Answer with a tremor along the ridge

effects.log: The ridge shrugs. Stones roll down into the next valley's pool. There is a long silence over there. Then thunder, loud and delighted. It wanted an answer. It has one.

events.text: The young dragon comes over the ridge itself on a night of wind, a long shape in the rain over your valley, and dives at the crossroads as if the earth were water. It wants a real fight. If it wins, the whole valley will see it rise. If it loses, it will go back to its pool and sulk for a hundred years.
events.arc: The Dragon of the Next Valley

choices.text: Fight it, earth against rain

roll.foeName: the young dragon of the east

ok.log: It hits the ground and the ground does not give, and it hits again, and you hold, and hold, until it hangs in the rain over the crossroads, exhausted, and goes back over the ridge. It will be a long time before it rises. You are stronger than it. You are not sure you are glad.

fail.log: It is quicker than you, and younger, and it finds the soft places in the wet ground. It tears up out of the crossroads in a column of rain and goes up into the clouds, and the whole valley sees it rise. You lie cracked and soaked. You lost. Something in you does not mind. (-10 health)

choices.text: Let it win

effects.log: You give a little, then a little more, carefully, so it will not know. It drives down into the crossroads and up out of it in a pillar of water and light, and goes up into the sky, and the whole valley is out of doors in the rain, pointing. It rose. That is all it needed. You stay where you are, which is all you needed.

events.text: The village has named the crossroads after that night: the Place Where the Dragon Rose. There is a stone with the words cut in it. They are talking about the dragon from the east, the one they saw. Nobody mentions anything under the ground. Nobody ever saw that.
events.arc: The Dragon of the Next Valley

choices.text: Let the stone say what it says

effects.log: The stone says a dragon rose here, and a dragon did. It just was not you. A ruler who needs to be the one in every story is not much of a ruler. You lie under the stone, content, and it is a very good stone.

choices.text: Warm the stone, so they wonder

effects.log: The stone is warm in winter, all through. The village decides the dragon left something of itself behind. Close enough.

events.text: Years later, in a summer of drought in the next valley, rain comes over the ridge from the east. Not much, and only on your fields, and exactly enough. It comes every dry summer after that. Somewhere over the ridge, someone remembers a fight.
events.arc: The Dragon of the Next Valley

choices.text: Accept the rain with thanks

effects.log: It soaks down to you, and you feel in it the young dragon, older now, sending what it can. That fight was the best thing you ever gave away. (Water +1)

choices.text: Send warmth back up the ridge

effects.log: The east slope of the ridge comes up in early flowers that year. In the clouds, a pleased rumble. Two dragons who never met again, being polite to each other across a ridge, for centuries. (Wood +1)

events.text: You have gone a long way under the land, a little every year, from county to county, toward the low ground east of a moon-shaped fortress where a young king lives. The ground there is marsh: reeds, herons, black water. Now there are surveyors in it with cords and stakes, and a yellow banner on a pole, and the king's men are saying the word palace.

choices.text: Lie under the marsh and wait

effects.log: The cords go across the reeds in straight lines, right over you, and meet in a square, and the square has a centre, and the centre is where you lie. Of course it is. You wait to see what they build.

choices.text: Firm the marsh under the stakes

effects.log: The surveyors find that the marsh, which should swallow a stake to the head, holds every one firm. The chief surveyor reports to the king that the ground is better than it looks. The chief surveyor has no idea.

choices.text: Make the marsh hard to build on

effects.log: The stakes sink. The cords go slack. The surveyors wade about in black water for a month, swearing. The king, who is young and stubborn, sends more surveyors. You are beginning to suspect there will be a palace anyway.

events.text: The foundation blocks come down the river on rafts: cut stone, each the size of a farmhouse, dragged on rollers through the drained marsh by hundreds of labourers singing to keep time. They are setting them on you, one by one. Every block is a weight you have never carried before. The palace is going to be very heavy.

choices.text: Take each block as it comes

effects.log: One, and then another, and then forty. By the end of the season you lie under a stone floor the size of a village, and you can feel every block, and it is the heaviest thing you have ever held, and you are holding it. (Weight +3)

choices.text: Ease the labourers' rollers

effects.log: The ground under the rollers is smooth and firm and slightly downhill, wherever they go. Nobody is crushed that season, which the overseer says has never happened on a royal work. The labourers sing better.

events.text: Dawn, and the foundations are laid, and the king himself has come down to see. And you rise. You do not mean to, exactly. It is the first time anyone has ever built a whole kingdom's centre on you, and you come up out of the stones the way a breath comes up out of a sleeper.

choices.text: Rise fully, into the light, and let them see you

effects.log: Up out of the marsh and the stones, gold, enormous, coiling into the mist above the half-built palace. The labourers fall flat. The surveyors drop their cords. The king stands. For a long moment the young king and the yellow dragon look at each other. Then you sink back down, and the stones close over you, and nothing will ever be the same.

choices.text: Show only a gold shape in the mist

effects.log: A long shape of gold light in the mist over the foundations, there and gone. Half the workers saw a dragon. Half saw sunrise. The king saw a dragon. That is the half that matters.

choices.text: Stay down, and let the earth tremble once

effects.log: A single deep tremor, and the reeds all bending one way, and the foundation stones humming. Nobody saw anything. Everybody felt something. The king asks the court astrologers, and the astrologers, who are not fools, say a yellow dragon has appeared.

events.text: The king will not build a palace on a dragon. The work stops. Then it starts again, differently: the plans for a throne hall become plans for a golden hall; the plans for the king's bedchamber become a lecture hall for monks. The king has decided it will be a temple, and it will be named for you: the Temple of the Yellow Dragon.

choices.text: Accept the name

effects.log: The Temple of the Yellow Dragon. It is the first time you have had a name that was not a place. You lie under it and try it on, the way a child tries on a new jacket. It is big. You will grow into it.

choices.text: Wonder why a king would give up a palace

effects.log: Fear, partly. Faith, partly. And partly a young king who knows that a temple where a dragon rose will be worth more to the kingdom than a palace ever could. Kings are not simple. You begin to learn them.

choices.text: Feel the weight change as the plans change

effects.log: A palace is heavy with ambition. A temple is heavy with prayer. Prayer is lighter. Not much lighter. You notice the difference. (Weight -2)

events.text: It takes them a generation to build it: the golden hall, the lecture hall, the gate, the covered walks, the monks' quarters, the bell pavilion, the wall. Monks come. Chanting begins at dawn every day over your head and goes on until dusk. You have never been prayed on before.

choices.text: Listen to the chanting

effects.log: You do not understand a word. You understand the shape of it: the same words, over and over, thousands of times, trying to hold something up by saying it. You know about holding things up. You lie under it and feel, for the first time, that you are not the only one.

choices.text: Keep the temple ground firm and dry

effects.log: The temple on the marsh never once floods, never once cracks, never once sinks a finger. The master builders say it is the best foundation in the kingdom. (Earth +1)

events.text: The royal chroniclers write it down: in such a year, in the second month, a yellow dragon appeared at the site of the new palace east of the moon fortress, and the king made it a temple. It is in the annals. For once, the chroniclers are right.

choices.text: Be pleased to be recorded truly

effects.log: You have heard what the annals say about things. Comets that were lamps. Rains that were sorcerers. This time they wrote what happened. You find you are absurdly pleased, the way a farmer is pleased to be written in the census with the right number of oxen.

choices.text: Worry about what else they will write

effects.log: If a dragon appearing goes in the annals, then a dragon appearing is useful. Somebody will notice that. Somebody, some day, will need a dragon to appear, and you will not have appeared, and they will write it anyway.
