events.text: A ship has drifted ashore on the south coast with nobody aboard: only a cargo of yellow iron and gold, three little clay models of holy figures, and a letter. The letter says a king of a far western land gathered this metal to cast great images and failed, and set it adrift to find a land where the casting would succeed. Every land it reached failed. The governor of the coast has sent it all to your temple.
events.arc: The Ship of Gold and Iron

choices.text: Feel the metal as it comes into the temple

effects.log: Gold and iron from the other side of the world, carried by a sea that did not care. It has been tried and failed over so many times it feels tired. It comes to rest over you like a traveller sitting down at last.

choices.text: Make the temple ready to receive it

effects.log: Earth bears metal. You draw yourself up under the casting yard of the temple, firm and dry and warm. If anywhere in the world can cast this, it is going to be here. (Metal +2)

events.text: The casting. A pit in the temple yard, a clay mould the height of three men, furnaces going for a week. The metal is poured, glowing. In the far western land it failed. In every land since, it failed. The founders stand round the pit without breathing.
events.arc: The Ship of Gold and Iron

choices.text: Hold the mould steady through the pour

ok.log: The ground does not shift a hair while the metal goes in. It cools. They break the mould. A great golden figure stands in the pit, whole, perfect, sixteen feet tall. The founders weep. You feel the metal settle at last, as if it had come home.

fail.log: A crack in the mould, a hiss of metal into the clay. You hold the rest. When they break it, the figure is whole except one hand, which they recast in the spring. It is still the first success anywhere in the world. (-6 health)

choices.text: Warm the mould from below so it cools evenly

effects.log: Slowly, slowly, for a month. It is the patience the far western founders did not have. When the mould is broken the figure is flawless, and the gold has a warmth to it that nobody can explain. (Fire +1)

events.text: The king who named your temple dies. That night, before anyone outside the palace knows, the great golden statue in your temple sheds tears: two lines of wet down its gilded face, to the floor. The monks find them at the dawn chant. They are terrified. They do not know it is because you wept first, under the floor, and the statue is standing on you.
events.arc: The Ship of Gold and Iron

choices.text: Let them see it, and wonder

effects.log: By noon the whole capital knows the statue wept, and by evening it knows why. From that day on, when the great statue weeps, the kingdom holds its breath. You did not mean to make an omen. You were only sad.

choices.text: Stop weeping, so the statue stops

effects.log: You go still and dry, with difficulty. The tears on the statue's face are drying by noon. The monks argue for a month about whether they saw it. They did. They will see it again. You cannot always stop.

events.text: The old abbot, {npc}, has worked it out. {npc} sits alone in the golden hall at night in front of the statue, and then gets down off the cushion and lies flat on the floor, ear to the stone, and says: it is not the statue, is it. It is you. Tell me what is coming next time, before you weep, so I can warn the king.
events.arc: The Ship of Gold and Iron

choices.text: Promise to tell

effects.log: "Yes," you say, the floor says, quietly. {npc} lies there a long time with eyes shut, and then gets up, and bows, and goes to bed. The next time grief is coming, the abbot knows a season early.

choices.text: Refuse: grief is not a warning service

effects.log: "I weep when I am sad," you say. "Not to be useful." {npc} sits up, and thinks about that, and laughs softly, and bows to the floor as to an equal. "Then I will just have to be sad with you," {npc} says.

choices.text: Say nothing, and stay warm under {npc}

effects.log: No word. Only warmth, coming up through the cold stone of the golden hall into an old body lying on it. {npc} falls asleep there, and is found at dawn by the novices, and refuses to explain.

events.text: A painter has come to your temple: {npc}, a farmer's child from the hills who taught themself to draw by scratching trees on rocks with a stick. {npc} is painting an old pine on the wall of the golden hall, and has been at it for a month, and it is the most alive thing you have ever seen on a wall.

choices.text: Warm the wall so the paint dries true

mem.note: dried my paint on the temple wall like sunlight

effects.log: The wall drinks the paint evenly, never too fast, never cracking. {npc} notices on the third day and stops, brush in the air, and looks at the wall, and then goes on painting faster, as if afraid it might change its mind.

choices.text: Watch how it is done

effects.log: Every needle is one stroke. Every crack in the bark is the side of a brush dragged once. {npc} paints the way you hold the ground: no stroke that is not needed, and every stroke holding the next one up.

events.text: The pine is finished, and the birds believe it. Sparrows, crows, a pair of magpies: they fly at the wall of the golden hall to land on the branches and hit the plaster and fall, stunned, onto the stone walk. The monks pick them up all day. The whole capital comes to see.

choices.text: Warn the birds through the wall

effects.log: The wall hums when a bird comes near, a low warm hum that a bird can feel and a monk cannot. The birds turn aside at the last moment, puzzled, and land on the roof instead, and stare at the pine. Nobody is hurt. The crowds are a little disappointed.

choices.text: Let them believe it

effects.log: They believe it, and fall, and the monks pick them up, and most of them fly away dazed. The painter becomes the most famous painter in the kingdom. You are not sure it is right. It is certainly true: the world believed a picture of itself.

choices.text: Soften the stone walk under the wall

effects.log: The flagstones under the painted pine are always warm and slightly soft, like moss. The birds fall and get up and shake themselves and fly. Some come back to try again. A pine, they seem to think, is worth a bump.

events.text: {npc} is old and comes to sit in front of the pine every evening. The paint has faded a little. The birds still come, fewer. {npc} has started talking to the wall, the way the old do, and tonight says: I always thought the wall helped me. Was it you?

choices.text: Answer: the pine was all yours

effects.npcPass: old age, in front of the painted pine

mem.note: said the pine was all mine

effects.log: "All yours," you say, from the floor. {npc} is very quiet. Then {npc} says thank you, to the wall or the floor or the pine, and goes to bed, and in the winter does not wake. The monks find a last little sketch of a sparrow by the bed.

choices.text: Answer: it was both of us

effects.log: "Both of us," you say. {npc} laughs, delighted, a farmer's child who painted with a dragon and was right to suspect it. The old painter dies that winter, smiling, people say.

events.text: Some years after the painter is dead, the pine has faded to a ghost, and the abbot has it repainted by a court painter with expensive green. It is a fine painting. It is a painting of a pine. The birds stop coming. Nobody notices for a year, and then everybody does.

choices.text: Grieve, quietly, under the wall

effects.log: You lie under the golden hall and feel the birds not coming. Something that was alive is now only correct. You will remember this when kings ask you to make things correct.

choices.text: Warm the new paint, to see if it wakes

ok.log: A single sparrow, one spring morning, flies at the new pine and bumps it and falls. Only one. The monks cheer. The court painter is insufferable about it for the rest of a long life.

fail.log: Nothing. Warm paint is still paint. Whatever the old painter put in that wall, you cannot put it back. It was never yours.

events.text: A little kingdom in the north has heard of the temple where a yellow dragon rose, and has named itself for you: the Kingdom of the Yellow Dragon. It is very small and very proud. Its king has sent a gift to a strong young prince of the great neighbour to the south, to test that prince: a bow so stiff no grown warrior in the little kingdom can draw it.
events.arc: The Bow of the Yellow Dragon Kingdom

choices.text: Wish the little kingdom well

effects.log: A kingdom named for you. It is a strange feeling, like hearing a stranger use your childhood name. You send a little luck north, to a land you will never lie under. It arrives as a mild winter.

choices.text: Worry about the test

effects.log: A gift that is a test is not a gift. A strong prince who is tested will want to prove it. You feel, from very far away, a quarrel beginning that will not be the little kingdom's to end.

events.text: Word comes south with the peddlers: the prince drew the bow, and drew it further, and broke it across one knee in front of the envoys, laughing, to show the little kingdom what it thought of tests. The little kingdom is ashamed. The prince's own father is angrier than the little kingdom is.
events.arc: The Bow of the Yellow Dragon Kingdom

choices.text: Feel for the prince, too strong for a father

effects.log: A strong heir is a danger to a father who is not as strong. You do not know this yet the way you will. You learn the first lesson of it now, from far away: the strongest child is not the safest one.

choices.text: Feel for the shamed little kingdom

effects.log: A small proud kingdom with a broken bow and nothing to say. You send it a good harvest. Pride heals better on a full stomach.

events.text: {npc}, the king of the little Yellow Dragon kingdom, has come all the way south to your temple in secret, alone but for two guards. {npc} kneels in the crypt at night and speaks to the floor. The prince's own father has written: the prince will visit to apologise; kill the prince while there. {npc} does not know what to do. {npc} came to ask the dragon the kingdom is named for.
events.arc: The Bow of the Yellow Dragon Kingdom

choices.text: "A guest is a guest. Send the prince home alive"

mem.note: told me to spare the prince

effects.log: {npc} weeps with relief, which tells you the answer was already there and only needed permission. The prince comes, and kneels, and the little king raises the prince up and sends the guest home with gifts. Whatever the father does next, it will not be by your kingdom's hand.

choices.text: "You must decide this. It is your house, not mine"

effects.log: {npc} sits back on the cold floor for a long time. Then gets up, and bows, and goes home, and when the prince comes, the little king looks at the young face and cannot do it, and sends the guest home with courtesy. It was always going to be that answer. It had to be the king's. (Weight -2)

choices.text: "Obey the great neighbour. A small kingdom survives by obeying"

effects.log: {npc} goes home grey-faced. When the prince comes, the little king means to do it, and looks at the young face, and cannot. The prince is sent home alive anyway. You said the wrong thing and a human did the right one. You carry that. (Weight +4)

events.text: Years later the peddlers bring the end of the story south: the strong prince went home, and the father did not forgive, and the prince's story ended badly, far away, by the father's order and not by any guest's knife. The little Yellow Dragon kingdom is long since swallowed by its neighbours. Its name is in one line of the annals.
events.arc: The Bow of the Yellow Dragon Kingdom

choices.text: Keep the little kingdom's name

effects.log: One line in the annals and one place at your middle. A small kingdom that was named for you, and at the one moment that mattered, would not kill a guest. That is a good thing to have been named after.

choices.text: Think about fathers and heirs

effects.log: A father who feared his son more than he loved him. You will lie under many fathers. You decide now, in the dark under the temple, that you will never take a side between a king and an heir. You will only stay with whoever is chosen. It is the only safe thing a centre can do.

events.text: A royal house stands on you now. {npc} sits on the throne a mile from your temple and the whole kingdom leans on that throne, and the throne leans on you. You can feel every edict as it is sealed. Do you hold this house up with everything you have, or keep a little distance, the way you keep the market's scale?

choices.text: Uphold the house: bless the ruler

effects.log: You settle under the palace and hold it up, and the harvests come in, and the borders hold, and the court calls it a fortunate reign. {npc} never knows why it is so easy. It is not easy for you. (Reign +3, Weight +2)

choices.text: Keep your distance: let the house stand on its own

effects.log: You stay under your temple, not under the palace. The house stands, a little shakily, on its own feet. You feel every wobble and do not catch it. It is very hard to watch. It is lighter.

choices.text: Watch {npc} for a year before you decide

effects.log: A year of edicts, of audiences, of meals, of moods. You learn how {npc} sleeps and what {npc} does when angry. A centre should know what it is holding up before it holds it.

events.text: The court has a habit now: when anything goes well, the ministers say it is the dragon's favour, and when anything goes badly, they say the dragon is displeased. {npc} has started asking the court astrologers every morning what the dragon thinks. The astrologers make it up.

choices.text: Make one of the astrologers dream the truth

effects.log: The youngest astrologer dreams of a great warm floor that does not have opinions about the price of salt. In the morning the young astrologer tells {npc} the truth: the dragon does not think about most things. {npc} is relieved, and the astrologers are furious.

choices.text: Let them make it up; it keeps the court careful

effects.log: A court that thinks a dragon is watching is a careful court. The lies are mostly harmless. You know, though, that one day somebody will make up something harmful, and say it was you. (Reign +2)

events.text: Something is wrong with {npc}. You felt it from the first winter: a coldness in the edicts, a pleasure in the sentences. Today a provincial governor who failed to collect a tax is to be put to death in the capital square, and the court says the dragon wills it.

choices.text: Shake the square, so the court is afraid

effects.log: The square heaves under the scaffold. The crowd scatters. The execution is put off, and off, and in the end the governor is exiled instead. {npc} is furious, and frightened, and that will not last. (Weight +2)

choices.text: Withhold the harvest blessing, so the court notices

effects.log: A thin harvest. The court murmurs that the dragon is displeased, and this time it is true. {npc} is not moved. A cruel ruler is not stopped by thin rice. (Reign -3)

choices.text: Endure it: you cannot leave a house yet

effects.log: Not yet. You are bound to this house by the palace stones over you, and you cannot leave it yet. You lie under the square while it is done. The weight of it settles on you like ash. (Weight +3)

events.text: A good year in the reign of {npc}: a bridge over the great river, a granary in every county, a law that a farmer's land cannot be taken for a debt. The court is very pleased with itself. You lie under the palace and feel the kingdom settle, the way a house settles after it is finished.

choices.text: Hold it all a little steadier

effects.log: The bridge stands. The granaries stay dry. The law is kept, mostly. You feel the house get heavier as it gets stronger, and you find you do not mind it yet. (Reign +3, Weight +2)

choices.text: Let the court have the credit

effects.log: It was their bridge and their law. You only kept the ground under them still. A ruler who can do good things without a dragon is worth more than one who cannot. You keep quiet.

events.text: The house has stood on you for a long time now. Rulers have come and gone; the throne is the same throne, the palace a little larger every reign. You find that you know the house the way a field knows its farmer: not its names, but its weight, and the way it walks.

choices.text: Bind yourself to the house for good

effects.log: You settle deeper under the palace. The house is yours and you are its, and the kingdom will remember this reign as the one when the dragon came to stay. It is a beautiful feeling. It is a very heavy one. (Reign +4, Weight +3)

choices.text: Remember that houses end

effects.log: Every roof you have lain under has been pulled down, outgrown or handed on: a farmhouse, a market, a yamen. This one will end too. You hold it up, and you keep one small place at your middle that is not holding it up, so that when it ends, something of you is left. (Weight -2)

events.text: Midnight. Somebody has come down the steps into the crypt under the golden hall, alone, with one candle: {npc}, the ruler, without guards or crown, in a night robe. {npc} kneels on the stone floor, right over you, and asks the floor a question as if expecting it to answer. 'They say this was to be my palace, and a dragon rose here. Then whose house is this?'

choices.text: "Yours, while you keep it well"

mem.note: spoke to me through the floor of the crypt

effects.log: It is the first thing you have ever said to a human in words. The voice comes up through the stone, slow and dry and much quieter than you expected. The candle shakes. {npc} does not run. {npc} says, very softly, "And if I do not keep it well?" You say nothing. That is also an answer. (Reign +2)

choices.text: "Mine. You are welcome in it"

effects.log: The first word you ever speak to a human, and it is a claim. {npc} bows to the floor, a deep bow, the bow of a guest to a host. From then on {npc} rules as a guest rules: carefully, and never quite at ease. (Weight +2)

choices.text: "The people's. We are both standing on them"

mem.note: said the house was the people's

effects.log: {npc} sits back on both heels and looks at the floor for a long time. "Then what are you?" {npc} asks. "The ground under the people," you say. "And what am I?" "The roof," you say. {npc} goes up the stairs in the dark, thinking, and does not sleep.

events.text: {npc} has come back to the crypt, as you knew {he} would, with a list. A drought in the south, a quarrel between two ministers, a border town that wants to go over to the neighbour. {npc} wants to know what the dragon would do.

choices.text: Answer one, and refuse the rest

effects.log: The drought, you answer: open the county granaries now, not later. The rest are the ruler's. {npc} is disappointed, and then, walking up the stairs, is not. A ruler who gets every answer from the floor is not a ruler. (Weight -2)

choices.text: Answer all of them

effects.log: You answer every one, well. The drought is eased, the ministers reconciled, the border town kept. {npc} comes back the next month with a longer list. And the next. You begin to understand where this goes. (Reign +3, Weight +4)

choices.text: Ask {npc} what {he} would do, and listen

effects.log: {npc} is startled, and then talks for an hour, and by the end has answered all three, mostly well. You say only "yes" twice and "think again" once. {npc} goes up the stairs taller. (Weight -1)

events.text: {npc} has a child now, and has brought the child down into the crypt at midnight to meet the floor. A small person in a silk jacket, clutching a candle with both hands, terrified and delighted. 'Say something,' {npc} whispers. 'Say something to the next one.'

choices.text: Say the child's name, kindly

effects.log: The child drops the candle. In the dark the child laughs, high and astonished, and {npc} laughs too, and for a moment the crypt under the Temple of the Yellow Dragon is a nursery. The heir will never be afraid of the dark.

choices.text: Say nothing: the child should not grow up needing a floor

effects.log: Silence. The child waits, disappointed. {npc} waits, puzzled. Then they go up, the child complaining. Later, much later, the heir will rule well and never once come down the crypt stairs. You chose that. (Weight -2)

events.text: {npc} is old and comes down the crypt stairs slowly, with a stick, one last time. {npc} sits on the floor, not kneeling, and puts both hands flat on the stone, and asks it again, the first question, as if the answer might have changed: 'Whose house was it?'

choices.text: "Yours. You kept it well"

mem.note: said I kept the house well

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly, as if hearing a verdict, and leans back against the crypt wall, and stays there until the novices come. Whatever else the annals say, this ruler heard it from the floor.

choices.text: "It was never anyone's. That is why it stood"

effects.log: {npc} laughs, an old dry laugh, and says, "I was afraid you would say that." And then, "Thank you." The old ruler goes up the stairs for the last time. The weight of a whole reign comes off your back as the footsteps go. (Weight -3)

events.text: {npc} has come down to the crypt at night again with a folded petition, as rulers of this house have learned to do. This year it is a rain that will not come, or a son who will not listen, or a minister who will not stop. {npc} lays the paper on the stone and waits.

choices.text: Grant it

effects.log: You do what is asked. It goes well. {npc} goes up the stairs lighter, and you feel the petition settle on your back with all the others. (Reign +2, Weight +3)

choices.text: Give it back: "This one is yours"

effects.log: The paper slides back across the stone toward {npc}'s knees. {npc} looks at it a long time, picks it up, and goes away to deal with it. Not every petition is a weight you have to take. (Weight -2)

choices.text: Answer with a question

effects.log: "What would you do if I were not here?" you ask. {npc} thinks, and answers, and it is a good answer. "Then do that," you say. It is the most useful thing a floor can say.

events.text: In a life that was not yours, somebody bought an honest scale for a market like this one, paid good coin for it, and set it in the middle of the square for anybody to use. The scale in front of you now is not that scale. But the beam of it hangs exactly level in the dawn, before anyone has touched it, as if it remembered.

choices.text: Keep the beam level, for whoever bought the first one

effects.log: A debt you never owed, paid forward in a thousand fair weighings. The beam hangs level every dawn for as long as you lie under that market. (Metal +1)

choices.text: Put the first grain on the pan yourself

effects.log: One grain of rice, from nowhere, on the pan at dawn. The beam does not move. A grain is too small to weigh. The market-keeper finds it, and leaves it there, and nobody ever brushes it off.

events.text: Somebody, in a life that was not yours, made a cheating merchant weigh his own false weights in front of the whole market, until he wept. You feel the shape of that day in this market's ground, like an old footprint under new mud. The cheats here are careful in a way they do not understand.

choices.text: Be glad of the footprint

effects.log: Fear keeps a market honest for a long time, and somebody planted it here for you. You do not have to be frightening. Somebody already was.

choices.text: Wish the shamed merchant had been forgiven, after

effects.log: Somebody wept in a market once, long before you, and was shamed for good reason. You hope somebody gave him a bowl of soup afterwards. You will try to be the kind of centre that remembers both halves.

events.text: Somebody, in a life that was not yours, once knelt in a market square in front of everybody and put a hand on the packed earth and said thank you to it. Nobody had ever said that to a market floor. You feel it now, in this ground, the way a field keeps the memory of a kind hand.

choices.text: Say it back, to the next person who kneels

effects.log: A child drops a coin and kneels to look for it in the dust. The ground under the small hand goes warm, and the coin is right there. The child says thank you without knowing why. You are even now, you think. Then you think you never will be.

choices.text: Keep the thanks at your middle

effects.log: You put it with the other warm things you keep at your middle. It is a very small thing to keep. It is one of the heaviest, in the good way.
